title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

  • recognise that different disciplines shape academic writing in distinct ways
  • identify how style, evidence, vocabulary, and discourse engagement vary across discipline families
  • evaluate and justify your own discipline's conventions
  • develop a critical edge by using the language of criticality to engage actively with sources.

title: Overview and justification
body:
This course assumes you already know how to structure a piece of academic writing and integrate sources. Now the question shifts: what does good writing look like in your discipline, and how do you develop the critical voice that distinguishes competent work from excellent?

You will explore how conventions vary across discipline families and learn to read your own discipline's expectations with sharper awareness.

title: Signpost
body: This course moves through four lessons, each building on the last: from recognising that disciplines differ, through analysing those differences, to applying that awareness to your own field and developing a critical edge.

_items.title: How disciplines shape writing
_items.body: You will explore how style, evidence, vocabulary, and discourse engagement vary across discipline families.

_items.title: Conventions in practice
_items.body: You will apply a four-point checklist to analyse academic writing and identify discipline conventions.

_items.title: Reading your own discipline
_items.body: You will turn the framework inward, examining how conventions work in your own field.

_items.title: The critical edge
_items.body: You will learn to signal critical engagement through the language of criticality.

_outro: Each lesson pairs teaching with a quick check or reflective task, so you can test your understanding and connect the ideas to your own writing.

title: Orientation
body: 'Academic writing' is not a single thing. Writing in chemistry looks different from writing in education, which looks different again from writing in history. Each discipline has its own conventions, characteristic features that shape how knowledge is presented. Once you can see these conventions, you can read for them in your own discipline and adapt your writing to fit.

title: Worked example
body:
Let's compare extracts from three disciplines: chemistry (representing the sciences), education (representing the social sciences), and history (representing the humanities). As you read, notice how the same four conventions (style, evidence, vocabulary, and discourse) manifest differently in each.

Style

In sciences writing, the style is often 'matter-of-fact': authors get to the point quickly, with short sentences that state things as they are. In our chemistry extract, sentences like 'Gram negative bacteria are in general more resistant than Gram positive' deliver findings without elaboration. This is not a flaw; it is the convention.

Social sciences writing is more discursive. Sentences are longer and more interpretive. In our education extract, the authors do not just report findings; they build connections: 'If outdoor learning provides children with freedom and opportunities to learn and problem solve.' The authors then connect this directly to the Framework's learning characteristics. Notice the tentative 'If': this is a contention, not a statement of fact.

Humanities writing is the most sophisticated in sentence structure. Our history extract uses semi-colons to connect independent clauses: 'Victorians had a complex relationship with their railways; they were simultaneously the ultimate symbols of progress.' The first clause provides context for the second.

Evidence

What counts as evidence varies dramatically. In sciences, the currency is data: quantitative results from chemical analyses, presented in tables. In social sciences, evidence often comes from policy documents and institutional reports; our education extract draws on Ofsted inspection reports and the Early Years Framework. In humanities, the primary evidence is the interpretations of other scholars. In our history extract, the author references Schivelbusch's work not just to situate the research but to shape the argument itself.

Vocabulary

Sciences use technical vocabulary precisely: 'Gram negative bacteria,' 'phenol components,' 'P. mirabilis.' These terms have exact meanings within the discourse community.

Social sciences use discipline-specific terminology too ('outdoor learning' in our extract) but also rely on tentative verbs: 'supports,' 'indicates,' 'suggests.' These signal that conclusions are interpretations, not certainties.

In humanities, vocabulary is harder to spot because the terms are not exclusive to the discipline. Words like 'complex,' 'anxieties,' and 'horrors' carry specific meaning in context. They recur because they are central to the argument.

Discourse engagement

All disciplines engage with existing scholarship, but how they do it differs. In sciences, references situate findings in context: the numbered citations [15,16] point to prior research that supports the current analysis. In social sciences, references are integral to the argument itself; Joyce's view is used to make a claim about the Framework's potential. In humanities, the views of other scholars are the substance of the discussion: the argument is built by engaging with what others have said.

The takeaway

These are not better or worse ways of writing; they are different conventions shaped by how each discipline produces knowledge. Sciences test hypotheses with data. Social sciences interpret evidence from multiple sources. Humanities build arguments through scholarly dialogue. Your task is to recognise which conventions apply in your discipline, so you can read for them and write within them.

title: Check: recognising discipline conventions
body:
Read this extract from a journal article:

'The findings indicate that parental involvement may contribute to improved outcomes, though the relationship is mediated by socioeconomic factors. Thompson (2019) suggests that engagement programmes are most effective when tailored to community context, a view supported by recent policy evaluations (DfE, 2022).'

Which discipline family does this writing most likely come from?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which discipline family does this extract most likely come from?

_items.text: Sciences: the style is matter-of-fact, and evidence comes from quantitative data.
Social sciences: the style is interpretive and tentative, and evidence includes policy documents.
Humanities: the style uses complex sentence structures, and evidence comes primarily from scholarly interpretations.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The tentative language ('may contribute,' 'suggests'), the use of policy documents as evidence (DfE, 2022), and the interpretive framing all signal social sciences conventions. Sciences writing would be more matter-of-fact with quantitative data; humanities writing would engage more directly with scholarly interpretations as the substance of the argument.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at the verbs ('indicate,' 'may contribute,' 'suggests') and the types of sources cited. What do these features tell you about the discipline's conventions?
_incorrect.final: This is social sciences writing. The tentative verbs ('may contribute,' 'suggests') and the use of policy documents (DfE, 2022) alongside scholarly references are characteristic of social sciences conventions. Sciences writing would be more matter-of-fact with quantitative data as the primary evidence; humanities writing would engage with scholarly interpretations as the substance of the argument, not just as supporting citations.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to apply a four-point checklist to analyse a piece of academic writing, using your observations about style, evidence, vocabulary, and discourse engagement to identify which discipline family the writing comes from.

title: Orientation
body: You have seen how style, evidence, vocabulary, and discourse engagement vary across discipline families. Now you need a practical way to use that knowledge. This lesson gives you a four-point checklist you can apply to any piece of academic writing, so you can read for convention and adapt your own writing to fit.

title: Concept introduction
body:
When you read academic writing in your discipline, look for four things:

1. Style: Are sentences short and matter-of-fact, or longer and more interpretive? Does the author state findings directly, or build connections between ideas?

2. Evidence: What counts as evidence here? Quantitative data? Policy documents? The interpretations of other scholars?

3. Vocabulary: What discipline-specific terms appear? Are there tentative verbs like 'suggests' or 'indicates'? Technical terms with precise meanings?

4. Discourse engagement: How does the author engage with existing scholarship? As context for findings? As integral to the argument? As the substance of the discussion itself?

These four questions form a checklist you can use whenever you read. The answers will tell you which conventions apply in that discipline.

title: Worked example
body:
Read this extract from a psychology journal article:

The results suggest that participants who engaged in the dual-task condition demonstrated significantly higher error rates than those in the single-task condition (M = 12.3, SD = 2.1 vs M = 6.8, SD = 1.9). This finding is consistent with cognitive load theory (Harrington, 1991), which posits that working memory has limited capacity. Chen and Martinez (2021) have similarly observed that attentional demands increase when individuals must process competing information streams.

Now let us work through the four-point checklist.

1. Style

The sentences are neither as clipped as sciences writing nor as elaborated as humanities writing. The first sentence states a finding with quantitative support; the second interprets it through theory; the third connects it to other research. This discursive but evidence-anchored style is characteristic of social sciences.

2. Evidence

The primary evidence is quantitative data from an experiment: mean scores and standard deviations. Unlike sciences writing, however, the data is not the endpoint. It leads into theoretical interpretation and connection with other studies. This blend of empirical data and interpretive framing is typical of social sciences research.

3. Vocabulary

Several terms signal the discipline: 'participants' (not 'subjects'), 'dual-task condition,' 'cognitive load theory,' 'working memory,' 'attentional demands.' These are technical terms with specific meanings in psychology. Notice also the tentative verb 'suggest' rather than a more definitive 'prove' or 'demonstrate conclusively.'

4. Discourse engagement

The author cites Harrington (1991) not just to situate the finding but to interpret it through an established theoretical framework. Chen and Martinez (2021) provide supporting evidence from parallel research. The discourse is integral to the argument, not merely contextual.

Synthesis

Applying the checklist confirms this is social sciences writing. The style blends empirical reporting with interpretation. The evidence combines quantitative data with theoretical framing. The vocabulary includes both technical terms and tentative verbs. The discourse engagement weaves existing scholarship into the argument itself. These are the conventions you would expect to see in psychology, and in social sciences more broadly.

title: Practical guidance
body:
The checklist works because conventions are not arbitrary. They reflect how each discipline produces knowledge. Sciences test hypotheses with data, so the writing is matter-of-fact and data-centred. Social sciences interpret evidence from multiple sources, so the writing is more discursive and tentative. Humanities build arguments through scholarly dialogue, so the views of other scholars are central.

When you read in your own discipline, use the checklist consciously at first. Over time, you will internalise the conventions and recognise them without needing to work through each point explicitly. The goal is disciplinary self-awareness: knowing what conventions apply in your field so you can write within them.

title: Check: recognising conventions
body:
Read this extract:

The data indicate that cortisol levels rose significantly following the stress protocol (t(42) = 3.87, p < .001). Similar patterns have been observed in studies of acute stress response (Taylor et al., 2019), though the magnitude of change may vary depending on individual differences in stress reactivity.

Which convention is MOST clearly demonstrated in this extract?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which convention is most clearly demonstrated in this extract?

_items.text: Style: The writing uses short, matter-of-fact sentences typical of sciences.
Evidence: The primary evidence is quantitative data from a controlled study.
Vocabulary: The extract uses discipline-specific terms with precise technical meanings.
Discourse engagement: The author builds the argument primarily through scholarly dialogue.

_feedback.correct: That is right. The most clearly demonstrated convention here is evidence. The extract leads with quantitative data (t-test results, p-value) from a controlled study, which is the primary basis for the claim. While the extract also shows social sciences style (interpretive framing, tentative 'may vary') and vocabulary ('cortisol levels,' 'stress protocol,' 'stress reactivity'), the evidence convention is most prominent because the statistical data is the centrepiece of the passage.

_incorrect.notFinal: Look again at what the extract leads with and builds from. Which convention provides the foundation for the author's claim?
_incorrect.final: The most clearly demonstrated convention is evidence. The extract leads with quantitative data (t-test results, p-value) from a controlled study. This statistical evidence is the centrepiece of the passage. While the extract also shows social sciences style and discipline-specific vocabulary, the evidence convention is most prominent here because the data provides the foundation for the claim. Style and vocabulary are present but secondary; discourse engagement is minimal (a single supporting citation rather than sustained scholarly dialogue).

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Evaluate a piece of discipline-specific academic writing against the four conventions of style, evidence, vocabulary, and discourse engagement.
  • Justify how your own discipline's writing typically satisfies (or departs from) these conventions, drawing on material you have read.
  • Critique your own current writing practice against the framework, identifying one convention to strengthen.

title: Orientation
body:
So far, you have learned to recognise how disciplines shape academic writing and practised applying the four-point checklist to an extract. Now it is time to turn that lens on your own field.

This lesson asks you to read for convention in your own discipline: to notice how style, evidence, vocabulary, and discourse engagement work in the writing you encounter every day. You will not analyse another example here; instead, you will bring what you already know from your reading and apply the framework to it.

title: Concept introduction
body:
Reading for convention means noticing how writing in your discipline works, not just what it says, but how it says it. The four-point framework gives you a structure for that noticing: style, evidence, vocabulary, and discourse engagement.

The questions below will guide you through each convention. Your discipline's conventions are what they are, and what matters is that you can identify them. Think about the journal articles, textbooks, or professional documents you read most often. What patterns do you see?

title: The four conventions in your discipline
instruction: Select each convention to consider how it appears in your discipline's writing.

_items.title: Style
_items.body:
What does your discipline's writing typically look like: short and matter-of-fact, or longer and more interpretive? Think about the journal articles or textbooks you read most often. Are sentences clipped and direct, or do they build through complex structures with embedded clauses?

How does that compare to what you have seen in other fields? If you have read across disciplines, you may have noticed that sciences tend toward brevity while humanities lean toward elaboration. Where does your field sit on that spectrum?

_items.title: Evidence
_items.body:
What counts as legitimate evidence in your discipline: quantitative data, case studies, primary texts, legal precedent, literature review? Think about the sources your tutors cite as authoritative and the kinds of support your assignments require.

How does that differ from what you have seen praised in other fields? A chemist's evidence looks nothing like a historian's, and both differ from what a lawyer would cite. Knowing what your discipline values helps you choose and present evidence appropriately.

_items.title: Vocabulary
_items.body:
What specialist terms does your discipline use that an outsider might not understand? Some are technical labels with precise definitions; others are ordinary words carrying discipline-specific meaning.

Think about the terms you have had to learn since starting your course. Are they names for specific things (like chemical compounds or legal doctrines), or are they familiar words used in unfamiliar ways (like 'discourse' or 'significance')? Both are part of your discipline's vocabulary, and using them correctly signals that you belong to the conversation.

_items.title: Discourse engagement
_items.body:
How do writers in your discipline engage with other scholars: primarily to situate their work in a field, to build an argument from prior findings, or to critique and challenge existing views? How central is that engagement to the writing itself?

In some disciplines, the scholarly conversation is the substance of the argument; in others, it is background context. Think about the articles you have read: do they foreground debate, or do they present findings as standalone contributions? Understanding this helps you position your own writing appropriately.

title: Practical guidance
body:
You now have a framework for reading your discipline's conventions. The next step is to use it actively.

Pick a piece of writing from your discipline (a journal article, a chapter, or a professional report) and work through the four conventions deliberately. Ask yourself: what is the style doing, what counts as evidence here, which vocabulary carries weight, and how does the author engage with other scholars? Write brief notes under each heading.

Do this once a week with a different piece, and you will build a working sense of what your discipline expects. That sense is what will eventually make your own writing feel native to the field.

title: Apply the framework
body: Think of a specific piece of academic writing you have read recently in your discipline. Name it briefly (author, title, or enough to identify it), then choose one of the four conventions (style, evidence, vocabulary, or discourse engagement) and describe how that convention appears in the piece.

title: Summary
body:
This lesson asked you to turn the four-point framework inward, to read for convention in your own discipline rather than in supplied examples. You considered how style, evidence, vocabulary, and discourse engagement work in the writing you encounter, and you applied the framework to a real piece from your field.

The framework is now a tool you can carry into your reading. Use it regularly, and you will build the disciplinary self-awareness that lets you write within your field's conventions rather than outside them.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Evaluate a passage of academic writing for its critical edge, distinguishing where the language of criticality signals active engagement with sources from where the writing merely reports them passively.
  • Justify why specific choices in presenting sources (leading with argument versus leading with source, presence versus absence of criticality markers) affect the perceived depth of a writer's engagement with discourse.
  • Revise a short passage so that it demonstrates a clear critical edge, integrating discourse markers (such as however, furthermore, moreover) and active source presentation to signal engagement with the relevant literature.

title: Orientation
body:
You have explored the four conventions that shape academic writing and considered how they appear in your own discipline. Now comes the final step: making your critical engagement visible to the reader.

Tutors often write 'be more critical' in feedback. What they usually mean is not that you lack critical thought, but that your writing does not signal it clearly enough. The difference between reporting sources and using them often comes down to a handful of words and phrases. This lesson shows you what those markers are and how to deploy them.

title: Concept introduction
body:
The critical edge in your writing is developed through the way you present interpretations. An active approach is needed: your argument comes first, and interpretations are then used to support and develop the point you are making.

The language of criticality is key here. Words like however, furthermore, therefore, and in addition do more than connect sentences. They signal relationships between ideas: contrast, addition, consequence, qualification. When a tutor reads these markers, they see evidence that you are not just listing sources but using them.

Developing this edge does not require drastic changes. It is subtle and nuanced. At the heart of it lies the issue of how you present the interpretations you have found, and your thoughts on them, to the reader. The examples that follow show the difference a few well-placed markers can make.

title: Worked example
body:
Read this passage about procrastination:

Procrastination is a problem for many students. Research has shown that it affects academic performance. Steel (2007) found that around 80–95% of students engage in procrastination. Kim and Seo (2015) looked at the relationship between procrastination and academic achievement. They found a negative correlation. Sirois (2014) examined how self-compassion affects the stress that procrastination creates. Students who procrastinate experience higher levels of stress. Tice and Baumeister (1997) suggested that procrastination provides short-term mood benefits. Students delay tasks to avoid negative emotions. Steel (2007) identified lack of self-regulation as a factor. Time management is also important according to several researchers (Häfner et al., 2014). Students need to understand why they procrastinate and develop strategies to address it.

This passage reports sources one after another but makes no argument. Each sentence describes what a researcher found, then moves on to the next. Notice what is missing:

  • No discourse markers signalling how sources relate (no however, furthermore, therefore)
  • No authorial voice: the writer never states their own point
  • No synthesis: sources are listed, not woven into an argument

The writing is not wrong, but it lacks a critical edge. A tutor reading it would ask: what is your point?

Now read the same content revised with a critical edge:

Research has consistently demonstrated that procrastination is a widespread challenge among university students, with studies suggesting that 80–95% engage in it at some point (Steel, 2007). However, recent work has moved beyond simply documenting its prevalence to examining why students procrastinate and what can be done about it. For example, early research framed procrastination as a time-management problem (Häfner et al., 2014). However, more recent studies emphasise its emotional dimensions: students delay tasks not because they lack planning skills but to avoid negative feelings (Sirois, 2014). Furthermore, this emotional avoidance may provide short-term mood benefits (Tice & Baumeister, 1997), which helps explain why procrastination persists despite its costs to academic achievement (Kim & Seo, 2015). This shift in understanding has therefore led researchers to advocate for emotion-regulation strategies rather than time-management interventions alone.

The same sources, the same evidence, but the writer makes a point. Notice the transformation:

BeforeAfter
Sources lead, argument absentArgument leads, sources support
No relationship markersHowever, For example, while, Furthermore, therefore
List of findingsSynthesis into a narrative (early view → recent shift → implication)

These discourse markers are the language of criticality. They signal to the reader that you are not just reporting what you found: you are using it.

title: Practical guidance
body:
The transformation you have just seen involved three moves:

  1. Lead with your argument. Open with an authorial claim that the sources will support, rather than with a source itself. Compare 'Steel (2007) found that...' to 'Research has consistently demonstrated that...'
  2. Use discourse markers. Words like however, furthermore, therefore signal relationships. They tell the reader you are doing something with the sources, not just presenting them.
  3. Build toward a judgement. The passage ends with a 'therefore' statement: a conclusion the writer draws from the evidence. That is the payoff of a critical edge.

You do not need to use every marker in every paragraph. One or two well-placed terms can shift a passage from passive to active. The key is intention: choose markers that reflect the relationship you actually see between ideas.

title: Check
displayTitle: Your turn: revise for critical edge
body:
Read this passage about online learning:

Online learning has become more common in higher education. Many universities now offer online courses. Allen and Seaman (2017) found that over 30% of students take at least one online course. Means et al. (2013) compared online and face-to-face instruction. They found that online learning can be as effective as traditional instruction. Garrison (2011) developed a framework for online learning communities. Student engagement is important. Dixson (2015) studied how students engage with online courses. Some students prefer online learning because of flexibility. Other students find it isolating. Universities need to consider how to support online learners effectively.

Revise this passage so that it has a critical edge. Your revision should:

  • Lead with your argument, not with sources
  • Use discourse markers (such as however, furthermore, therefore) to signal relationships between ideas
  • Synthesise the sources into a point, rather than listing them

Guidance: A passage with a critical edge typically opens with an authorial claim, uses markers like 'however' or 'furthermore' to signal relationships, and ends with a judgement. No single right answer exists, but the transformation should be visible.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about the last piece of academic writing you submitted or are working on now. Looking back, would you say it had a critical edge, or did it lean toward listing sources rather than using them? If you were to revise one paragraph, which discourse marker (however, furthermore, therefore) would most strengthen it, and why?
instruction: If you would like, jot down your thoughts below. This is for your own reflection and will not be marked. Select Submit to save your response; it will be here when you return.

title: Summary
body:
The critical edge in academic writing is not about dramatic changes. It is about how you present interpretations: leading with your argument rather than with sources, using discourse markers to signal relationships, and building toward a judgement.

Words like however, furthermore, and therefore are the language of criticality. They tell the reader you are doing something with what you have found, not just reporting it. A few well-placed markers can shift a paragraph from passive listing to active engagement.

This is the final lesson in the Academic Writing: Advanced stage. You have explored how disciplines shape writing, examined the four conventions in practice, applied them to your own field, and now learned to signal your critical engagement through language. The next step is to bring these strands together.

title: Question 1: Discipline conventions
body: Which of the following best describes how the sciences discipline family typically handles evidence?
ariaQuestion: How does the sciences discipline family typically handle evidence?

_items.text: Evidence is primarily quantitative data from experiments or observations, presented matter-of-factly.
Evidence comes from policy documents, institutional reports, and qualitative interpretation.
Evidence consists mainly of scholarly interpretations that form the substance of the argument.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Sciences typically rely on quantitative data from controlled experiments or observations. The data is presented directly, often with statistical measures, and forms the foundation for any claims made. This contrasts with social sciences (which blend empirical data with qualitative interpretation) and humanities (where scholarly interpretations are central).

_incorrect.final: Sciences typically rely on quantitative data from experiments or observations, presented matter-of-factly. Policy documents and institutional reports are more characteristic of social sciences. Scholarly interpretations as the main evidence are typical of humanities.

title: Question 2: Four-point checklist
body: A passage foregrounds the writer's personal reflection and uses hedged language throughout. Which discipline family does this most closely resemble?
ariaQuestion: Which discipline family does writing that foregrounds personal reflection with hedged language most closely resemble?

_items.text: Sciences: the hedged language reflects tentative findings from controlled experiments.
Social sciences: the interpretive framing and tentative language reflect this discipline's conventions.
Humanities: the personal reflection indicates engagement with scholarly interpretations.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The combination of personal reflection and hedged, tentative language is characteristic of social sciences writing. Social sciences often involve interpretation of evidence where conclusions are rarely black and white, hence the tentative framing. Sciences tend toward matter-of-fact statements about data; humanities engage more with scholarly debate than personal reflection.

_incorrect.final: Social sciences writing often features personal reflection combined with hedged, tentative language. This reflects the interpretive nature of social sciences research where conclusions involve judgement rather than proof. Sciences writing is more direct and data-focused; humanities writing centres on scholarly dialogue rather than personal reflection.

title: Question 3: Evaluate conventions
body: An extract from an academic text omits citations entirely and relies on logical deduction from first principles. Which convention does this satisfy, and which does it undermine?
ariaQuestion: If an extract omits citations and relies on logical deduction, which convention does this satisfy and which does it undermine?

_items.text: Satisfies style (matter-of-fact reasoning); undermines discourse engagement (no connection to scholarly conversation).
Satisfies evidence (logical deduction is evidence); undermines vocabulary (no technical terms used).
Satisfies discourse engagement (building an argument); undermines style (too informal for academic writing).

_feedback.correct: That's right. Logical deduction from first principles can satisfy the style convention (direct, matter-of-fact reasoning). However, omitting citations entirely undermines discourse engagement, which requires connecting your argument to the scholarly conversation. In academic writing, even logical arguments typically need to be situated within existing discourse.

_incorrect.final: Logical deduction from first principles can satisfy the style convention through direct, matter-of-fact reasoning. But omitting citations entirely undermines discourse engagement. All discipline families expect writers to connect their work to existing scholarship, even when building logical arguments. Discourse engagement is about showing how your work relates to what others have said.

title: Question 4: Critical edge
body: Which of the following sentences demonstrates active engagement with sources rather than passive reporting?
ariaQuestion: Which sentence demonstrates active engagement with sources rather than passive reporting?

_items.text: Smith (2020) found that students who plan their essays perform better.
Research shows that essay planning improves performance (Smith, 2020; Jones, 2021).
However, as Smith (2020) demonstrates, planning alone is insufficient without revision strategies.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The third sentence shows active engagement through several markers: 'However' signals a contrast with a previous point; 'as Smith demonstrates' frames the source as evidence for an authorial claim; and 'planning alone is insufficient' presents a judgement rather than just reporting findings. The other options report what researchers found without building an argument.

_incorrect.final: The third sentence shows active engagement: 'However' signals contrast, 'as Smith demonstrates' frames the source as evidence for a claim, and 'planning alone is insufficient' presents a judgement. Sentences that simply report what researchers found (Smith found, research shows) are passive reporting. Active engagement uses discourse markers and presents sources as evidence for the writer's own argument.

title: In real academic practice
body: These ideas apply directly to your next piece of writing. Before you submit, ask: does my writing show awareness of my discipline's conventions? Does my critical voice come through, or am I merely reporting what others have said?

title: Where this goes next
body: This is the final stage of the Academic Writing pathway. What you have learned here (reading for convention, developing a critical edge) will serve you across every writing task your degree requires.
